subject: Banking
title: Overdraft Fees: A $30 Billion Business
description: A fast breakdown of Overdraft Fees: A $30 Billion Business for builders.

hook.text: US banks collected $30 billion in overdraft fees in a single year. A $5 coffee that overdraws costs you $35.

buildup.text: Overdraft protection sounds helpful. But it charges $35 each time you spend more than your balance, sometimes daily.

discovery.text: Banks reorder transactions to maximize overdraft fees.

twist.text: 80% of overdraft fees are paid by 9% of customers, usually the poorest account holders living paycheck to paycheck.

climax.text: Overdraft fees are a regressive tax on poverty. The less money you have, the more the bank charges you.

punchline.text: $30 billion from overdrafts. The poorest customers pay the most.

quiz.question: Who pays the most overdraft fees?
options: About 9% of customers, usually the poorest

details.summary: Overdraft fees generated over $30 billion annually at their peak by charging $35 per transaction when accounts went negative. Banks maximized this revenue by reordering transactions to trigger the most possible overdraft charges per day.
details.whyItMatters: Overdraft fees represent one of banking's most controversial profit centers, extracting money from the customers least able to afford it. Regulatory and competitive pressure has reduced but not eliminated these practices.
takeaways: Banks earned over $30 billion annually from overdraft fees at peak
Transaction reordering maximized the number of overdraft charges per day
A single $5 overdraft could trigger a $35 fee, a 700 percent implicit charge

faq.question: How did transaction reordering increase overdraft fees?
faq.answer: Banks processed the day's largest purchases first, quickly draining the account, then charged $35 for each subsequent small transaction. Five $10 purchases with a $50 balance could trigger four overdraft fees of $35 each, totaling $140.

faq.question: Are overdraft fees declining?
faq.answer: Yes. Regulatory pressure, negative publicity, and neobank competition have reduced industry overdraft revenue. Many large banks have lowered fees, added grace periods, or eliminated overdraft charges entirely. Revenue has dropped from $30 billion to under $10 billion.
